title: Hackers send false nuclear alerts through Ukrainian and Russian warning apps
dek: Ukraine's Air Alert app warned of an incoming Oreshnik missile late on Sunday; hours later Russia's Emergencies Ministry app told users that nuclear warheads had been launched. No one has claimed either attack.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Hackers broke into the emergency warning apps of both Ukraine and Russia within hours of each other, sending users false alerts of nuclear attack, in a new front of the war that opened as a local truce in southern Ukraine came to an end.

Ukraine's Air Alert app, which tells people when to take shelter from Russian missiles and drones, was compromised late on Sunday, 1 November. Early on Monday, Russia's Emergencies Ministry said its own mobile app had been hit by "a massive cyberattack" that let attackers send fake warnings to the public. No group has claimed either attack, and no casualties or injuries have been reported.

## What happened in Ukraine

Users of Ukraine's Air Alert app received a Russian-language notification that read, in one report's translation: "Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is on its way." The Oreshnik is a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile. The app also showed false warnings of chemical and radiological hazards and of street fighting in Kyiv, according to another report.

Ukraine's Air Force said on Telegram that the app "appears to have been subjected to enemy influence", adding: "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm." The app's developers said "unauthorized persons have interfered with the application", and that they had turned off push notifications and suspended it. The false alerts were cleared after about an hour, reports said, and the developers said at about 2 am that the app was gradually being restored and that it stores no personal data. Ukraine's Digital Transformation Ministry said sirens and other warning channels were working normally, one report said.

Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia, reports said. Regional governors in Ivano-Frankivsk and Vinnytsia called it a cyberattack and told residents not to click on links in the messages.

## What happened in Russia

In the early hours of Monday, users of the Russian Emergencies Ministry's app received messages claiming that nuclear warheads had been launched across all regions of Russia and telling them to stock up on food for three weeks and shelter in basements, according to one report. Another report said similar messages appeared on regional ministry channels, with reports from St Petersburg, the Moscow region, Belgorod, Nizhny Novgorod, Sverdlovsk and Tyumen.

"The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," the ministry said on Telegram. It said work was under way to fix the vulnerability and urged people to "remain calm and trust only official sources of information". The ministry did not say who it believed was responsible. The Kremlin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said on Monday that the president's website and other government agencies faced cyberattacks "many times a day, every day".

One report suggested the Russian hack may have been a Ukrainian response; another said it was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.

## Background

The attacks came just after the end of a local humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky, in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson region, which one report described as the longest truce of the war so far. Ukraine says nearly 800 people were evacuated during the pause, while Kyiv and Moscow have accused each other of using it to move troops.

Both countries have also stepped up long-range strikes. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 433 drones at Ukraine on Sunday and 193 more overnight into Monday, while Ukrainian drones have set fire to Russian oil refineries at Kstovo and in the Samara region.

## Why it matters

Warning apps are a lifeline in both countries, where people rely on them to decide when to take shelter. False alerts that cry wolf can erode trust in genuine warnings, and those that invoke nuclear weapons can cause panic. The incidents show how the war's cyber battle has moved from government websites and broadcasters to the tools ordinary people use to stay alive.

## What happens next

Both apps were being restored on Monday. Neither government has published a technical account of how the systems were breached.
